objectives: Explain what scarcity means and why it forces every person and every society to make choices.
Distinguish the basic economic questions (what, how, and for whom to produce) and describe how traditional, command, market, and mixed economies answer them.
Explain how specialization and the division of labor let us produce more with the same resources.

concepts.definition: The condition in which the resources available to make or get what people want (time, money, labor, land, materials) fall short of what people want. Scarcity is why we have to choose.
The study of how individuals, businesses, and societies make choices under scarcity.
With limited resources, getting more of one thing means getting less of something else. Whenever a budget or the time available is fixed, trade-offs appear.
What to produce and how much, how to produce it, and for whom to produce it (who gets what). Every society has to answer these questions.

The ways a society answers the basic economic questions: a traditional economy (by custom), a command economy (by government planning), a market economy (by voluntary trade between buyers and sellers), or a mixed economy (by markets and government together). Most countries today have mixed economies.
Splitting work into separate tasks so that each person focuses on one of them. Workers gain skill and use tools more efficiently, so the same resources produce more output.

beginner.summary: You want lots of things, but your time and money are limited. So you always have to pick what to do, and that is where economics begins.

sections.heading: Why do we have to choose?
paragraphs: Everyone gets 24 hours a day, and your spending money is limited. You can't have every movie you want to see, every book you want to buy, and every snack you want to share with friends. When what you have falls short of what you want, that is called scarcity.

Scarcity isn't just a problem for people with little money. Rich people also get only 24 hours a day, and every country has a limited amount of land, workers, and money. Economics is the study of how people and societies decide how to use scarce resources, such as time, money, land, and workers, that are not enough to satisfy all their wants.

sections.heading: Choosing one thing means giving up another
paragraphs: If you play soccer with friends on Saturday afternoon, you can't spend that time on homework. If you spend your money on sneakers, you can't use that same money on a video game. When getting more of one thing means getting less of another, that is a trade-off.

sections.heading: Societies have to choose, too
paragraphs: Your school is no different. With this year's budget, it has to decide whether to fix the gym, buy library books, or improve the cafeteria. Countries face even bigger questions: What should we make, and how much? How should we make it? Who gets it?

Societies answer these questions in different ways. Some decide the way things have always been done (traditional). Some let the government plan (command). Some let buyers and sellers decide through trade (market). Most countries today have a mixed economy, where markets and the government decide together.

sections.heading: Splitting up the work makes more
paragraphs: Imagine your class is making sandwiches for a school fair. If each person does every step alone, from slicing the bread to wrapping, it goes slowly. If you split the jobs (one person slices, one adds fillings, one wraps), everyone gets faster and nobody wastes time switching tasks, so the class makes more sandwiches. This is called division of labor and specialization. Because the same people and ingredients make more, it is also a way to make scarce resources go further.

intermediate.summary: Scarcity forces choices, and every choice involves a trade-off. Societies answer the basic economic questions through their economic systems and increase output through specialization and the division of labor.

sections.heading: Scarcity and economics
paragraphs: Scarcity does not mean "there is only a little of something." It means "there is less than people want." In most places, ordinary outdoor air is available to everyone in the amount they want at no cost, so it is not scarce (although clean air can be scarce in heavily polluted cities). Clean water is abundant on Earth as a whole, yet it is scarce in regions where demand exceeds the supply. Economics analyzes the criteria that individuals, businesses, and governments use to choose under scarcity and how those choices affect one another.

sections.heading: Trade-offs
paragraphs: When budgets, time, and resources are fixed, choosing more of one thing necessarily means less of another. Understanding this relationship frees you from the illusion that you can do everything and lets you compare what is worth giving up, and how much. The next lesson measures the value of what you give up more precisely, using the idea of opportunity cost.

sections.heading: The basic economic questions and economic systems
paragraphs: Every society must decide what to produce and how much (the types and quantities of goods), how to produce (with which technologies and resources), and for whom to produce (who gets how much).

A traditional economy follows custom and the practices of earlier generations. In a command economy, the government decides through central planning. In a market economy, outcomes emerge from voluntary trade among many buyers and sellers. Most real-world countries have mixed economies: market trade is the default, while the government sets rules and provides public services. The main difference among these systems is who makes the decisions: custom, the government, individual buyers and sellers, or a combination of markets and government.

sections.heading: Specialization and the division of labor
paragraphs: When work is divided and each person focuses on one task, (1) repetition builds skill, (2) less time is lost switching between tasks, and (3) it becomes easier to use tools and techniques suited to that task. As a result, the same number of workers and the same materials can produce more. However, specialized workers must exchange what they produce with one another, so the division of labor develops hand in hand with trade.

advanced.summary: Choice under scarcity can be modeled as a constrained optimization problem. Each allocation method strikes a different balance between efficiency and equity, and specialization expands the production constraint itself.

sections.heading: Choice under constraints
paragraphs: Economics treats a choice as a problem: maximize an objective (satisfaction, profit, or social welfare) without exceeding the constraint set by available resources (budget, time, technology). Scarcity simply means that such a constraint exists. Without constraints there would be no problem of choice, and no need for economics. If you spend a budget m on two goods with prices p₁ and p₂, the constraint is p₁x₁ + p₂x₂ ≤ m. When the whole budget is already spent (p₁x₁ + p₂x₂ = m), increasing x₁ by one unit requires reducing x₂ by p₁/p₂ units. If part of the budget is still unspent, you can buy more x₁ without giving up any x₂ until the budget runs out. This ratio expresses the trade-off in quantitative terms.

sections.heading: Comparing allocation methods
paragraphs: Scarce resources can be allocated by price (markets), by plans and rules (government), by custom (tradition), first come, first served, by lottery, or according to need. Allocation by price tends to send goods to those who value them most and can be efficient, but people who cannot pay may go without even when their need is great. First come, first served makes people pay with time (waiting in line) instead of money, and a lottery looks fair but may not send goods to those who need them most. A mixed economy manages these trade-offs by allocating most goods through markets. The government intervenes in areas where equity matters most, such as health care, education, and a minimum standard of living.

sections.heading: Specialization and expanding production possibilities
paragraphs: Because the division of labor yields more output from the same inputs, it pushes outward the range of combinations a society can produce (the production possibilities frontier, covered in the next lesson). Adam Smith used the example of a pin factory to illustrate the productivity gains from the division of labor. Excessive specialization, however, also has costs: monotonous work, dependence on a single region or industry, and vulnerability when exchange is disrupted. The risks of supply-chain disruptions are revisited in the global economy course (c08).

worked_examples.title: Can you afford both?
worked_examples.problem: Hypothetical example: You have $20 of spending money left this month. A movie ticket you want costs $12, and a comic book you want costs $9. How much more money would you need to buy both?
worked_examples.answer: You are $1 short, so you have to pick one of the two. This is a choice caused by scarcity.

worked_examples.title: How the division of labor raises output
worked_examples.problem: Hypothetical example: Three students are making sandwiches for a school fair. If each student makes sandwiches alone from start to finish, each one makes 4 sandwiches per hour. If they split the work into slicing, filling, and wrapping, the three of them together make 18 sandwiches per hour. By how many sandwiches, and by what percentage, does the division of labor increase hourly output?
steps: Output of three students working alone: 4 × 3 = 12 sandwiches.
Output with the division of labor: 18 sandwiches.
worked_examples.answer: Output rises by 6 sandwiches (50%). With the same people and the same ingredients, dividing the work produces more.

worked_examples.title: Budget constraint and the rate of exchange
worked_examples.problem: Hypothetical example: A school club has an activity budget of $120. A ball costs $20, and a snack pack costs $8. (1) If the club buys 4 balls, what is the maximum number of snack packs it can buy? (2) What is the opportunity cost of one more ball, measured in snack packs (the price ratio)?
steps: (2) One more ball costs another $20. In snack packs, that is $20 ÷ $8 = 2.5 packs.
The price ratio (p_ball / p_snack = 20/8 = 2.5) is the number of snack packs given up to get one more ball.
worked_examples.answer: (1) 5 snack packs. (2) 2.5 snack packs: one ball costs as much as 2.5 snack packs. This is a rate of exchange, not a number of packs the club can actually buy. Because packs cannot be split, buying a 5th ball leaves $20, enough for only 2 packs, so the club actually gives up 3 packs; buying 2 more balls means giving up exactly 5 packs.

real_world_examples.title: Where the idea that specialization boosts output began
paragraphs: In The Wealth of Nations, a classic of economics, Adam Smith illustrated the power of the division of labor with a pin factory: once the work was split into many separate steps, each worker's output rose dramatically. Today's factories, restaurant kitchens, and software teams divide work on the same principle.

real_world_examples.title: Economic systems around the world
paragraphs: Pure traditional, command, or market economies are rare in practice. Most countries have mixed economies in which market trade is the default and the government intervenes through laws and regulations, taxes, and public services. The balance between markets and government differs from country to country.

sdg_case.title: A limited school budget: where should the resources go?
paragraphs: SDG 12 aims for sustainable consumption and production. SDG target 12.2 calls for the sustainable management and efficient use of natural resources.

Hypothetical scenario: Your school has a fixed facilities budget for this year, and the student council must propose how to spend it. Because the budget is scarce, choosing one project means postponing the others until next year.

options.name: Replace classroom lighting with energy-efficient lights
benefits: Electricity use and power bills fall, so the money saved each year can be spent elsewhere.
It is a visible example of using resources efficiently.
costs: The up-front installation cost is high.
Other facility improvements that money could have paid for must wait.
assumptions: The electricity savings are as large as expected, and the lights stay in use for many years.

options.name: Switch to more reusable cafeteria trays and cups and upgrade the dishwashing equipment
benefits: Less single-use waste is thrown away.
Students experience sustainable consumption every day.
costs: Washing requires more water, electricity, and staff time.
There is some disruption while the equipment is installed.
assumptions: The reusable items are used enough times that the resources saved exceed the resources used to make them.

options.name: Buy library books and learning equipment
benefits: Students' learning opportunities increase right away.
costs: It does little to save resources.
The other two projects must wait.
assumptions: Students actually make heavy use of the new materials.

discussion: With a fixed budget, which criterion (cost savings, the environment, learning, or fairness) would you put first when ranking the three projects? How does the ranking change depending on the criterion you choose?

key_takeaways: Scarcity means resources fall short of what people want, so every individual and every society must make choices.
Every society must decide what, how, and for whom to produce, and each economic system (traditional, command, market, mixed) answers these questions differently.
Specialization and the division of labor let the same resources produce more, but they require exchange and cooperation and create a risk of dependence.
